DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Status of Claims
This office action is in response to the patent application 17/181,544 originally filed on February 22, 2021. Claims 1-20 were originally presented for examination.
A preliminary amendment was filed on February 22, 2021 in which claims 1-20 were canceled and claims 21-36 were presented as new claims. Claims 21 and 27 are independent.
Claims 21-36 remain pending.
Information Disclosure Statement
The Information Disclosure Statement filed on March 12, 2021 has been considered. The foreign patent document Cite No 1 was not considered because no English translation or abstract was submitted. An initialed copy of the Form 1449 is enclosed herewith.
Priority
This application is a continuation of US application 16/834,898, filed March 30, 2020. This application has a US provisional application 62/827,557, filed April 1, 2019.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), in which the patent or application, as the case may be, names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claims 27-29 and 34 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by Ive et al. (hereinafter “Ive,” US 2024/0012601).
Regarding claim 27, Ive discloses a therapeutic training device, comprising:
eyeglass frames (Ive [0003], “HMDs take various forms, including goggles, helmets, masks, visors, glasses…”);
an outward facing video display positioned within the eyeglass frames (Ive [0044], “The embodiments herein are generally directed to head-mounted displays (HMDs), and more particularly, to HMDs that have an outward-facing output system (including display(s), a speaker(s), or the like)”; also Ive [0146], “these concepts apply equally or by analogy to head mounted displays or wearable electronic devices or systems of other configurations as well, including without limitation visors, glasses…”); and
a controller coupled to the outward facing video display to control a display of media content on the video display, such that the display of media content is viewable by a patient with the therapeutic training device is worn by a user (Ive [0055], “The HMD 102 also includes an external or outward-facing display 106. The outward-facing display 106 may define a display surface that faces away from the wearer, and may be configured to display visual output (e.g., still images, video images) to persons other than the wearer 100. As noted above and described herein, such visual output may include real-time or pre-captured video or still images of at least a part of the wearer's 100 face (e.g., the wearer's eyes and eyebrows).”).
Regarding claim 28, Ive discloses that the outward facing video display is a video projector, a LCD display, a LED display, or a quantum dot display (Ive [0127], “The outward-facing display 106 may be any suitable type of display, including a liquid-crystal display (LCD), organic light emitting diode (OLED) display, LED display, or the like.”).
Regarding claim 29, Ive discloses that the outward facing video display comprises a plurality of outward facing video displays (Ive [0129], “while the outward-facing display 106 is often shown and described herein as a single display component, it may include multiple different displays, such as two or more displays in a side-by-side arrangement, or two or more displays in an over-under arrangement.”).
Regarding claim 34, Ive discloses eye tracking components and software (Ive [0142], “The HMD 2000 may also include wearer-facing sensors 2024 that may be used to sense, capture, and/or detect information about a wearer of the head-mounted display (including video and/or still images). Example wearer-facing sensors 2024 include, without limitation, cameras, eye-tracking sensors”).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 21-26, 35, and 36 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Ive in view of Saur et al. (hereinafter “Saur,” US 2018/0308451), and in further view of Samec et al. (hereinafter “Samec,” US 2016/0270656).
Regarding claim 21, and substantially similar limitations in claim 35, Ive discloses a therapeutic training device comprising a head mounted display having an outward facing video display (Ive [0044], “The embodiments herein are generally directed to head-mounted displays (HMDs), and more particularly, to HMDs that have an outward-facing output system (including display(s), a speaker(s), or the like)”).
Ive does not explicitly teach a video display comprising a transparency that is variable.
However, Saur discloses a video display comprising a transparency that is variable (Saur [0016], “modifying a degree of transparency of at least one playback arrangement of the head-wearable presentation apparatus”; also Saur [0017], “a head-mounted display (also referred to as HMD) is understood to be a visual output appliance that is worn on the head. It presents images on a display of the playback arrangement. By way of example, the display can be a display arranged in front of the eyes, the degree of transparency of which for optical signals can be modified by applying a voltage… The degree of transparency of the display, of the reflection area or of the device for reducing ambient light that is incident on the beam splitter can be set, in particular, in a range from 0% (opaque) to 100% (transparent) as desired.”).
Saur is analogous to Ive, as both are drawn to the art of head mounted displays. It would be obvious to try by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to have modified the method as taught by Ive, to include a video display comprising a transparency that is variable, as taught by Saur, because it combines prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results. Doing so is a predictable solution that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued with a reasonable expectation of success.
Ive in view of Saur does not explicitly teach a head mounted display comprising a light having an adjustable brightness to illuminate the eyes of a wearer.
However, Samec discloses a head mounted display comprising a light having an adjustable brightness to illuminate the eyes of a wearer (Samec [1858], “The augmented reality/virtual reality device can comprise a head mounted display… The generated thin illuminating beam can be conditioned by one or more lenses and filters and directed into the eye of a user… the angle of incidence and/or the brightness of the thin illuminating beam on the eye can also be adjusted…”).
Samec is analogous to Ive in view of Saur, as both are drawn to the art of head mounted displays. It would be obvious to try by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to have modified the method as taught by Ive in view of Saur, to include a head mounted display comprising a light having an adjustable brightness to illuminate the eyes of a wearer, as taught by Samec, in order to provide imaging output of various portions of the wearer’s eyes for ophthalmic use cases (Samec [1858]). Doing so is a predictable solution that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued with a reasonable expectation of success.
Regarding claim 22, and substantially similar limitations in claim 36, Ive does not explicitly teach a controller configured to inversely adjust the transparency of the outward facing video display and the brightness of the light.
However, Saur discloses a controller configured to inversely adjust the transparency of the outward facing video display (Saur [0016], “modifying a degree of transparency of at least one playback arrangement of the head-wearable presentation apparatus”; also Saur [0017], “a head-mounted display (also referred to as HMD) is understood to be a visual output appliance that is worn on the head. It presents images on a display of the playback arrangement. By way of example, the display can be a display arranged in front of the eyes, the degree of transparency of which for optical signals can be modified by applying a voltage… The degree of transparency of the display, of the reflection area or of the device for reducing ambient light that is incident on the beam splitter can be set, in particular, in a range from 0% (opaque) to 100% (transparent) as desired,” the transparency of the display can be adjusted to be more opaque or more transparent).
Saur is analogous to Ive, as both are drawn to the art of head mounted displays. It would be obvious to try by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to have modified the method as taught by Ive, to include a controller configured to inversely adjust the transparency of the outward facing video display, as taught by Saur, because it combines prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results. Doing so is a predictable solution that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued with a reasonable expectation of success.

Samec is analogous to Ive in view of Saur, as both are drawn to the art of head mounted displays. It would be obvious to try by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to have modified the method as taught by Ive in view of Saur, to include a controller configured to inversely adjust the brightness of the light, as taught by Samec, in order to provide imaging output of various portions of the wearer’s eyes for ophthalmic use cases (Samec [1858]). Doing so is a predictable solution that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued with a reasonable expectation of success.
Regarding claim 23, Ive in view of Saur and Samec discloses that the outward facing video display a video projector, a LCD display, a LED display, or a quantum dot display (Ive [0127], “The outward-facing display 106 may be any suitable type of display, including a liquid-crystal display (LCD), organic light emitting diode (OLED) display, LED display, or the like.”).
Regarding claim 24, Ive in view of Saur and Samec discloses that the outward facing video display comprises a plurality of outward facing video displays (Ive [0129], “while the outward-facing display 106 is often shown and described herein as a single display component, it may include multiple different displays, such as two or more displays in a side-by-side arrangement, or two or more displays in an over-under arrangement.”).
Regarding claim 25, Ive in view of Saur and Samec discloses eye tracking components and software (Ive [0142], “The HMD 2000 may also include wearer-facing sensors 2024 that may be used to sense, capture, and/or detect information about a wearer of the head-mounted display (including video and/or still images). Example wearer-facing sensors 2024 include, without limitation, cameras, eye-tracking sensors”).
Regarding claim 26, Ive does not explicitly teach a controller configured to adjust a transparency of the outward facing video display, and adjust the brightness of the light.
However, Saur discloses a controller configured to adjust a transparency of the outward facing video display (Saur [0016], “modifying a degree of transparency of at least one playback arrangement of the head-wearable presentation apparatus”; also Saur [0017], “a head-mounted display (also referred to as HMD) is understood to be a visual output appliance that is worn on the head. By way of example, the display can be a display arranged in front of the eyes, the degree of transparency of which for optical signals can be modified by applying a voltage… The degree of transparency of the display, of the reflection area or of the device for reducing ambient light that is incident on the beam splitter can be set, in particular, in a range from 0% (opaque) to 100% (transparent) as desired,” the transparency of the display can be adjusted to be more opaque or more transparent).
Saur is analogous to Ive, as both are drawn to the art of head mounted displays. It would be obvious to try by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to have modified the method as taught by Ive, to include a controller configured to adjust a transparency of the outward facing video display, as taught by Saur, because it combines prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results. Doing so is a predictable solution that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued with a reasonable expectation of success.
Samec discloses a controller configured to adjust the brightness of the light (Samec [1858], “The augmented reality/virtual reality device can comprise a head mounted display… The generated thin illuminating beam can be conditioned by one or more lenses and filters and directed into the eye of a user… the angle of incidence and/or the brightness of the thin illuminating beam on the eye can also be adjusted,” the brightness of the light can be adjusted to both brighter and dimmer).

It would be obvious to try by one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to have modified the method as taught by Ive in view of Saur, to include a controller configured to adjust the brightness of the light, as taught by Samec, in order to provide imaging output of various portions of the wearer’s eyes for ophthalmic use cases (Samec [1858]). Doing so is a predictable solution that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued with a reasonable expectation of success.
Claim 30 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Ive in view of Samec.
Regarding claim 30, Ive does not explicitly teach a light having an adjustable brightness to illuminate the eyes of the user.
However, Samec discloses a light having an adjustable brightness to illuminate the eyes of the user (Samec [1858], “The augmented reality/virtual reality device can comprise a head mounted display… The generated thin illuminating beam can be conditioned by one or more lenses and filters and directed into the eye of a user… the angle of incidence and/or the brightness of the thin illuminating beam on the eye can also be adjusted…”).

Doing so is a predictable solution that one of ordinary skill in the art could have pursued with a reasonable expectation of success.
Claims 31-33 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Ive in view of Saur.
Regarding claim 31, Ive does not explicitly teach that a transparency of the media content displayed on the outward facing video display is adjustable.
However, Saur discloses a transparency of the media content displayed on the outward facing video display is adjustable (Saur [0016], “modifying a degree of transparency of at least one playback arrangement of the head-wearable presentation apparatus”; also Saur [0017], “a head-mounted display (also referred to as HMD) is understood to be a visual output appliance that is worn on the head. It presents images on a display of the playback arrangement. By way of example, the display can be a display arranged in front of the eyes, the degree of transparency of which for optical signals can be modified by applying a voltage… The degree of transparency of the display, of the reflection area or of the device for reducing ambient light that is incident on the beam splitter can be set, in particular, in a range from 0% (opaque) to 100% (transparent) as desired.”).

Regarding claim 32, Ive does not teach that the transparency of the media content displayed on the outward facing video display is adjusted manually by the user.
However, Saur discloses the transparency of the media content displayed on the outward facing video display is adjusted manually by the user (Saur [0031], “an actuation unit for modifying a degree of transparency of at least one playback arrangement of the head-wearable presentation apparatus”; also Saur [0034], “The evaluation unit and/or the actuation unit can be integrated into the head-wearable presentation apparatus or realized as software on a computer.”).

However, Saur discloses the transparency of the media content displayed on the outward facing video display is adjusted by software (Saur [0031], “an actuation unit for modifying a degree of transparency of at least one playback arrangement of the head-wearable presentation apparatus”; also Saur [0034], “The evaluation unit and/or the actuation unit can be integrated into the head-wearable presentation apparatus or realized as software on a computer.”).
